references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says exactly the same thing: "I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, but revealed them to little children."
Psalm 8:3 speaks of God establishing a song of praise from the mouths of children and infants, which reflects the theme that God reveals his truth to the simple rather than the wise.
Isaiah prophesies that the wisdom of the wise will perish and the understanding of the understanding be hidden – this corresponds with God having hidden these things from the wise and understanding.

Paul quotes and expounds on the theme that God makes the world's wisdom into foolishness and has chosen to save through what the wise consider foolish, which mirrors Jesus' praise that God hides truth from the wise.
Paul speaks of a wisdom that the rulers of this age did not know, because God had hidden it – a theme that directly connects to Jesus' words that the Father has hidden these things from the wise.
"Praise the Lord, for he is good" – the expression ἐξομολογοῦμαί σοι (I praise you) reflects the Old Testament tradition of praise and confession toward God.
Melchizedek blesses Abram by "God Most High, Maker of heaven and earth" – the title "Lord of heaven and earth" is an ancient name for God that Jesus here uses for his Father.
The immediate context: The seventy return with joy because demons are subject to them. Jesus responds with this song of praise, showing that God's revelation is given to simple disciples.
Jesus tells Peter that "flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven" – it is the Father who reveals truth to those he wills, not human wisdom.

Jesus explains that it has been given to the disciples to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but not to others – this expands on the theme that God reveals his truths to the chosen and hides them from others.
David's praise "Praise the Lord, my soul" reflects the joy and praise in the Spirit that Jesus expresses in this verse.
Paul speaks of God having predestined us according to his own free purpose – the expression "it was your good pleasure" (εὐδοκία) connects to God's sovereign will in the plan of salvation.
Isaiah speaks of God blinding eyes and hardening hearts – this shows that it is God's sovereign action to hide and reveal truth.
